name: Converting the Letter Grade of a Student to It's Numeric Range
description:
Construct a program that receives a grade from the user and prints the numeric range for that grade using the following grading rules:
A for scores ≥ 90
B for scores ≥ 80
C for scores ≥ 70
D for scores ≥ 60
F for scores < 60
For example, if the user enters the grade D, the program prints "Score is in range [60-70)".

2.content: grade = input("Enter a grade letter in uppercase: ")
commentList: You read a line of text from the user with input('Enter a grade letter in uppercase: ') and store that text in the variable grade; this provides the letter the rest of the program will inspect.
You use the assignment operator = to bind the string returned by input() to the name grade; input(...) is a function call and the argument is the prompt string shown to the user.
You should know that input(...) waits for the user to type something and press Enter, then returns a Python string (not a number); the returned string does not include the newline character.

Common mistakes: you might enter a lowercase letter like 'd' or include extra spaces so comparisons like grade == 'D' fail; pressing Enter with no text gives an empty string; forgetting quotes around the prompt or parentheses causes syntax or NameError.

Best practices: normalize and validate the input right away, for example grade = input('...').strip().upper() to remove surrounding whitespace and convert to uppercase, and then check that grade is one of the allowed letters before using it.
If you ever run this on Python 2, note that input behaves differently (it evaluates the entered text); in modern Python 3 input returns a string, so use input as shown.

distractors.description: You might pick this because in many contexts you use a single = to set a value, so it can feel natural to try the same inside a condition. Step-by-step: (1) You write a single '=' hoping to check if the input is A. (2) The interpreter reads it as an attempt to assign the string to a name inside the if statement, which is not allowed in this language. (3) The program will fail to run and raise a syntax error before any of the print statements execute. Why this is tempting: beginners often mix up assignment and comparison operators because they look similar and both involve '='. How this affects the program: instead of moving on to check the grade and print the correct range, the program stops with an error. What's missing or wrong: the line uses the assignment operator rather than the proper equality-check operator required in a conditional, so it does not perform a comparison and is invalid syntax.

You might use this because you want to check for either uppercase or lowercase A and think you can just join the two values with or. Step-by-step: (1) You write the condition expecting it to mean "grade equals 'A' or grade equals 'a'". (2) The language interprets the second part as a plain non-empty string, which is always truthy. (3) As a result, the whole condition always evaluates as true, so the program always takes this branch no matter what the user enters. Why this is tempting: it looks shorter and reads like natural language, so students often try it. How this affects the program: instead of correctly matching only when the grade is A, the program will always print the A message, giving incorrect output for B, C, D, and F. What's missing or wrong: you must perform a comparison for each value or normalize the input first; simply placing another literal after or does not compare the variable to that literal.

You might pick this because in math you write a = b and think that tests equality, or because some other languages allow assignment inside conditions. In Python, using a single = here causes a syntax error: the interpreter expects a comparison, not an assignment, so the program will fail to run and you'll get a SyntaxError. If you replace the correct comparison with this assignment form, the program will not execute at all, so it won't print any grade ranges. The key issue is that this line attempts to assign rather than test equality; the needed behavior is to check whether the grade variable equals the letter, not to assign a value to it. That's why this choice is invalid even though it looks similar to a correct conditional.
